difficultyRationale: Platform-estimated: MODERATE — a single deductive-logic setting that needs 2–3 steps of case analysis (which pair plays first, who must win game 2, who wins game 3) with routine checking; about 2–3 minutes.
stem:
Rishi and Swathi are students of Class 5. Pavan and Tanvi are students of Class 4. Rishi and Pavan are boys. Swathi and Tanvi are girls. The four students played a total of three games of chess. The games were played one after another. A player who lost a game did not participate in any more games. It was observed that:

(i) the first game was the only game where two students of the same class played against each other,

(ii) the students of Class 5 won more games than the students of Class 4, and

(iii) the boys won two games and the girls won one game.

The student who did not lose any game is \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_.

solution.quick: The winner of game 1 must also win game 2. Otherwise the last two players would be classmates in game 3. That double winner must be from Class 5 by (ii) and a boy by (iii), so it is Rishi. The girls' single win must then be game 3, won by a Class‑4 girl, Tanvi. Tanvi never loses, which is option **(D)**.

steps.title: Set up the structure
steps.body:
| Student | Class | Gender |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Rishi (R) | 5 | Boy |
| Swathi (S) | 5 | Girl |
| Pavan (P) | 4 | Boy |
| Tanvi (T) | 4 | Girl |

Condition (iii) counts 3 wins (2 by boys, 1 by girls) in 3 games, so every game has a winner and a loser. A loser plays no further game, so the 3 games have **3 different losers**. Exactly **one** student never loses, and that student is the answer. Each game is played between two students who have not yet lost.

steps.title: Game 1 is between classmates — test the Class 4 pair
steps.body:
By (i), game 1 is either **R vs S** (Class 5) or **P vs T** (Class 4), and games 2 and 3 must be between different classes.

**Suppose game 1 is P vs T**, with winner $W$ (Class 4). The players still in are $W$, R and S.

- Game 2 must be cross-class, so it is $W$ vs R or $W$ vs S.
- If $W$ loses game 2, the two remaining players are R and S, both from Class 5. Game 3 would then be a same-class game, which contradicts (i).
- If $W$ wins game 2, Class 4 has won games 1 and 2, i.e. at least 2 of the 3 games. That contradicts (ii).

So game 1 **cannot** be P vs T. **Game 1 is Rishi vs Swathi.**

steps.title: Game 1 = R vs S: its winner must also win game 2
steps.body:
Let $W \in \{R, S\}$ be the winner of game 1. The players still in are $W$, P and T.

- Game 2 must be cross-class: $W$ vs P or $W$ vs T.
- If $W$ lost game 2, the remaining players P and T (both Class 4) would meet in game 3, which contradicts (i).

So $W$ **wins game 2**, and game 3 is $W$ against the other Class 4 student. Class 5 then already has 2 wins, so (ii) holds whatever happens in game 3.

steps.title: Apply the gender condition (iii)
steps.body:
- If $W$ = Swathi, the girls win games 1 and 2, i.e. 2 games. That contradicts (iii), which allows the girls only one win.
- So $W$ = **Rishi**. The boys have now won games 1 and 2, i.e. both of their allowed wins. **Game 3 must therefore be won by a girl.** Game 3 is Rishi against a Class 4 student, and the only Class 4 girl is **Tanvi**. So game 2 was Rishi vs Pavan (Rishi won), and game 3 is Rishi vs Tanvi, won by Tanvi.

The unique sequence is:

| Game | Players | Winner | Loser | Same class? |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Rishi vs Swathi | Rishi | Swathi | Yes |
| 2 | Rishi vs Pavan | Rishi | Pavan | No |
| 3 | Rishi vs Tanvi | Tanvi | Rishi | No |

Check: (i) ✓. (ii) Class 5 won 2 games, Class 4 won 1 ✓. (iii) boys won 2 (both by Rishi), girls won 1 (Tanvi) ✓.

steps.title: Identify the student who never lost
steps.body: The losers are Swathi (game 1), Pavan (game 2) and Rishi (game 3). The only student who never lost is **Tanvi**, option **(D)**. An exhaustive search over all possible game sequences finds this as the only consistent scenario.

solution.teaching:
This is a **deductive logic** puzzle with an elimination format: the loser of each game leaves and the winner stays to play the next game, like *king of the hill*. Two structural facts make such puzzles quick.

1. **Count the losers.** Every game eliminates exactly one player, so $k$ decisive games among $k+1$ players leave exactly **one** unbeaten player. The question "who never lost?" therefore has a unique answer once the sequence is known.
2. **Track who is still in.** Before each game, list the players who have not lost. A condition such as "only game 1 was between classmates" limits which pairs may meet later. In particular, if the last two players left are classmates, the final game breaks the condition.

**Method: case analysis with early pruning.** Branch on the smallest decision (who plays game 1). For each branch, find the move that is *forced*, such as "the game‑1 winner must also win game 2". Then apply the counting conditions (wins by class, wins by gender) to kill branches. Stop as soon as one consistent scenario remains, and re-check it against every condition.

Here the class structure forces one player to win both games 1 and 2. The win counts identify that player as a Class 5 boy, i.e. Rishi. That leaves exactly one girl's win for game 3. Since Rishi then loses, the unbeaten player is **Tanvi**, the student who played only the final game. The trap is to assume the most successful player (Rishi, 2 wins) must be the one who never lost.

optionAnalysis.label: A
optionAnalysis.explanation: Pavan loses game 2 to Rishi. For Pavan to stay unbeaten, he would have to beat the player who won games 1 and 2 in game 3. If that player is Rishi, the boys win all 3 games. If it is Swathi, the girls already have 2 wins. Both cases contradict (iii).

optionAnalysis.label: B
optionAnalysis.explanation: Rishi wins games 1 and 2 (both boy wins). If he also won game 3, the boys would have 3 wins, contradicting (iii). He must lose game 3 to Tanvi.

optionAnalysis.label: C
optionAnalysis.explanation: Swathi loses game 1 to Rishi. If Swathi won game 1, she would also have to win game 2, giving the girls 2 wins and contradicting (iii).

optionAnalysis.label: D
optionAnalysis.explanation: Tanvi plays only game 3 and beats Rishi. This is the girls' single win and Class 4's single win, consistent with (i)–(iii). She is the only student who never loses.

solution.shortcut: The game‑1 winner must win game 2 as well, otherwise game 3 would be between classmates. A player with two wins must be from Class 5 (ii) and a boy (iii), so it is Rishi. The girls' one win must come in game 3 against Rishi from a Class 4 girl, so it is Tanvi.
solution.commonTrap: Picking **Rishi** because he wins the most games. Rishi's two wins use up the boys' quota, so he must lose the final game. The unbeaten student is Tanvi, who played only once.

answerVerification.method: Author solve (not blind) compared with official key
answerVerification.notes: A hand case analysis and an exhaustive search over all elimination sequences of 3 decisive games give one consistent scenario (R beats S, R beats P, T beats R), with Tanvi unbeaten. This agrees with official key D. Assumption used: every game is decisive, which follows from (iii) counting 3 wins (2 by boys, 1 by girls) in 3 games.
